source: In addition, these cell surface antigens have been demonstrated to have direct effects on the susceptibility for several diseases (Franchini et al., 2012; Stowell and Stowell, 2019a; Stowell and Stowell, 2019b).

claim: Individuals with blood group O have a decreased risk of thromboembolic events.
source: Multiple subsequent studies have revealed associations with a range of diseases, with a prominent example being a decreased risk of thromboembolic events and increased risks of some hemorrhagic events in individuals with blood group O (Franchini et al., 2012; Edgren et al., 2010; Vasan et al., 2016a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Individuals with blood group O have increased risks of some hemorrhagic events.
source: Multiple subsequent studies have revealed associations with a range of diseases, with a prominent example being a decreased risk of thromboembolic events and increased risks of some hemorrhagic events in individuals with blood group O (Franchini et al., 2012; Edgren et al., 2010; Vasan et al., 2016a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: ABO status may explain as much as 30% of the variability in levels of Factor VIII and von Willebrand factor.
source: The difference in thrombotic and hemorrhagic phenotypes has been attributed to variability in levels of Factor VIII and von Willebrand factor, where ABO status may explain as much as 30% of this variability (Franchini et al., 2012; Orstavik et al., 1985; Germain et al., 2015; Lindström et al., 2019; O'Donnell et al., 2002)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The allele distribution of blood group antigens has evolved to reflect some areas endemic to infectious diseases.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The ABO gene is located on chromosome 9.

claim: The A and B allelic variants of the ABO locus encode the A and B glycosyltransferases, which differ only by a few amino acid residues.
source: The A and B allelic variants of the ABO locus encode the A and B glycosyltransferases, which differ only by a few amino acid residues, add the donor substrates UDP-N-acetylgalactosamine or UDP-galactose, respectively, to a common acceptor substrate, namely a carbohydrate chain terminating with the so-called H antigen, in turn dependent on fucosyltransferase activity expressed from the FUT1 and FUT2 genes on chromosome 19.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the molecular biology of ABO blood groups.

claim: In blood group O, the H antigen is left unaltered due to lack of ABO enzyme activity, most commonly by a single-nucleotide deletion in the ABO coding region.
source: In blood group O, the H antigen is left unaltered due to lack of ABO enzyme activity, most commonly by a single-nucleotide deletion in the ABO coding region (Storry and Olsson, 2009).

claim: Multiple testing was handled using a two-stage approach with FDR adjustment in the main cohort and Bonferroni adjustment in the validation cohort.

First, in the exploratory analysis using the main cohort, we applied a false discovery rate (FDR) adjustment of raw p-values assuming positive dependency of stochastic ordering between outcomes. Second, in the confirmatory analysis using the validation cohort, we used the disease categories with significant effects from explorative analysis, with results presented both without adjustment and using a Bonferroni adjustment.
